translation: The endless sea noise did not cease for a minute.
It surged in long waves, intensifying and then dying down.
And the wind would start to rustle in the bare trees, then fall silent, just as I did while listening to the flow of the night.
But he did not leave, he was here.
I knew this by the smell of wet pebbles and by the barely perceptible tremor of a solitary plane tree leaf.
I had noticed this stubborn grey leaf during the day, but now at night, it seemed to me a small living creature, my only wakeful friend.
From time to time, gunshots could be heard from the darkness, from the city.
After each shot, the dogs barked for a long time.
Then a faint light flashed far out at sea and went out.
He made us look at these things more attentively and for longer than we usually do, discovering many qualities in them that had previously gone unnoticed.

Thus, in the porous yellow stone there were many small seashells firmly embedded into it, on the thistle bushes there were still a few flowers left, they sat on straight sturdy stems looking like soaked and wrinkled golden butterflies, patiently waiting for the sun.
But it rarely appeared through the fog as a blurred white spot, providing neither heat nor shade.
Under the solitary old plane tree with lemon spots on its trunk, leaves lay scattered around, as if cut out of dull green velvet.
Through the iron gate ants were running in a line, carrying into their underground granaries the last provisions for winter, while a small timid toad lived under the anchor chain.
During the night, someone on the other side of the river began to wave a lantern and shout at length.
I went out with my uncle.
Ilko to the shore.
The river roared.
Water flowed through the dam in a cold waterfall.
The night was late and silent, not a single star was overhead.
The fresh wildness of the spilled river and thawed earth was blowing in my face.
All the time, someone on the other shore was waving a lantern and shouting, but their words couldn't be heard over the noise of the river.
When the coffin was carried out to the porch, I saw on the far side of the river an old carriage, horses unharnessed and tied to it, and a small woman in black mother.
She stood motionless on the shore.
From there, she saw her father being taken away.
Then she knelt down and fell with her head onto the sand.
No, grandfather replied.
That's true, we haven't seen each other.
Ostap began to go blind.
He then decided to go as far as Petersburg to see that woman before he went completely blind.
He reached the royal capital and learned that she had died, presumably unable to bear the separation.
Ostap found her white marble tombstone in the cemetery, looked at it, and his heart broke on the stone lay his iron rose.
That woman had bequeathed to have a rose placed on her grave.
Forever.
And Ostap began to wax lyrical and probably died on the road or in the market under a wagon.
Amen!
On the other bank, Countess Branitsky's protected forest was climbing up the slope.
The sun could not break through the dense greenery of this forest.
Only occasionally would a solitary beam cut diagonally through the thickets, revealing to us the stunning power of vegetation.
Tiny birds flew into this beam of light like sparkling specks of dust.
They were squealing, chasing each other and diving into the foliage as if it was green water.
I filled a bucket with water from the pond, threw some grass into it, and waited.
The red floats stood motionless in the water.
Then one of them would start to quiver, make light circles, suddenly dive or quickly swim to the side.
Father made a strike, the fishing line tightened, the walnut rod bent into an arc, and over the misty pond the splashing and fuss started.
The water rippled, rocking the lily pads, water beetles hurriedly scurried in all directions, and finally a flickering gold shimmer appeared from the mysterious depths.
It was impossible to figure out what it was until my father dragged a heavy crucian carp onto the trampled grass.
He lay on his side, panting and moving his fins.
An amazing scent of the underwater kingdom came from his scales.
Yasha was counting seconds to himself.
We knew that it took seven minutes to walk from Sturdza Lane to the Landesman Sanatorium.
In the sanatorium behind a high fence and iron gates, we always felt completely safe.
Especially if incense was not lit.
When we were passing by the gateway, Yasha tripped.
Later, when we reminisced about the incident in Sturdza Lane, Yasha insisted that every time you aim to do something in the best possible way, you inevitably mess up on some trifle.
But as for me, I thought that Yasha's unbearable gait was to blame for everything.
But I remained silent so as not to upset Yasha.
We sneaked down the alley.
I said that we need to go on the side where the gate is, not reaching it, stop and listen carefully, then quickly and silently dash past the gate.
The calculation, in my opinion, was mathematically accurate.
If there are people in the alley, they might not notice us.
If we were to walk on the opposite side from the alley, we could be noticed from far away.
I calculated that in the latter case we would be walking past the dangerous alleyway, or rather, be in sight of people who were hiding in the alleyway, five times longer.
And therefore, there will be five times more chances that we will be noticed.
In the morning, I was woken up by the hot sun shining on the white walls.
Red and yellow hollyhocks swayed behind the open window.
A nasturtium flower was peeking into the room with them; a furry bee sat in it.
Frozen, I watched as she angrily retreated and extracted herself from the tight flower.
Bright streams ran endlessly across the ceiling, light waves reflecting from the river.
The river was roaring right there, nearby.
